title: Asymmetry of verification and verifier's rule
pub: jasonwei.net (personal blog; author then at OpenAI, subsequently Meta Superintelligence Labs)
author: Jason Wei

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

mo.t: Evaluation validity: Benchmark safeguards impose trade-offs
Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
Professional tasks: Partial credit overstates complete success
Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

kp.k: Verification costs vary substantially across tasks
kp.d: Wei presents asymmetry of verification as a framework for understanding AI progress: some tasks are substantially easier to check than solve, others require comparable effort, and some are harder to verify than to propose. Examples range from puzzles and BrowseComp searches to arithmetic, code review, essay fact-checking and scientific hypotheses. This is a cross-domain conceptual argument, not a study of legal work.
qs: Asymmetry of verification is the idea that some tasks are much easier to verify than to solve.
Some tasks have near-symmetry of verification: they take a similar amount of time to verify as to write a solution.
For example, it might take longer to fact-check all the statements in an essay than to write that essay
For example, it is easy to state a novel diet (“Eat only bison and broccoli”) but it would take years to verify whether the diet is beneficial for a general population.

kp.k: Upfront research can reduce subsequent verification effort
kp.d: Wei argues that verification difficulty is partly changeable through advance preparation. Answer keys make checking final mathematical answers trivial, while sufficiently comprehensive test cases accelerate checking code. Such preparation does not always eliminate checking effort: a list of famous Dutch soccer players would assist, but not exhaust, verification of possible answers.
qs: it is possible to actually improve the asymmetry by front-loading some research about the task.
for a competition math problem, it is trivial to check any proposed final answer if you have the answer key at hand.
if you have test cases with ample coverage, you can quickly check any given solution; indeed, this is what Leetcode does.
In some tasks, it is possible to improve verification but not enough to make it trivial.

kp.k: Verifier’s rule predicts AI success on verifiable tasks
kp.d: Wei proposes that the ease of training AI is proportional to task verifiability, reasoning that checking solutions enables creation of reinforcement-learning environments. His assertion that all solvable, easily verified tasks will be solved by AI is a prediction, rather than an established finding or a quantified relationship demonstrated in the document.
qs: In RL terms, ability to verify solutions is equivalent to ability to create an RL environment.
Verifier’s rule: The ease of training AI to solve a task is proportional to how verifiable the task is. All tasks that are possible to solve and easy to verify will be solved by AI.*

kp.k: Five verification properties favour AI training
kp.d: Wei identifies agreement about good solutions, checking within seconds, parallel verification, low-noise signals correlated with quality, and the ability to rank solutions through continuous rewards as favourable conditions. These concern verification and reward generation for AI training, rather than specifically human checking before professional reliance.
qs: Objective truth: everyone agrees what good solutions are
Fast to verify: any given solution can be verified in a few seconds
Scalable to verify: many solutions can be verified simultaneously
Low noise: verification is as tightly correlated to the solution quality as possible
Continuous reward: it’s easy to rank the goodness of many solutions for a single problem

kp.k: Benchmark success supports the rule in Wei’s argument
kp.d: Wei cites his broad observation that most proposed AI benchmarks are easily verified and have been solved as support for the rule, without providing a systematic benchmark inventory or measured success rate. He says virtually all popular benchmarks in the past ten years meet the first four properties, while binary rewards can be averaged across examples to produce a continuous reward.
qs: most benchmarks that have been proposed in AI are easy to verify and so far have been solved.
Notice that virtually all popular benchmarks in the past ten years fit criteria #1-4; benchmarks that don’t meet criteria #1-4 would struggle to become popular.
although most benchmarks don’t fit criteria #5 (a solution is either strictly correct or not), you can compute a continuous reward by averaging the binary reward of many examples.

kp.k: Fast, informative feedback enables greater learning
kp.d: Wei’s proposed mechanism is that the five properties permit many gradient steps with strong learning signals. He attributes faster progress in digital than physical environments to iteration speed, explicitly presenting the learning explanation as his view.
qs: In my view, the most basic reason is that the amount of learning that occurs in neural networks is maximized when the above criteria are satisfied; you can take a lot of gradient steps where each step has a lot of signal.
Speed of iteration is critical—it’s the reason that progress in the digital world has been so much faster than progress in the physical world.

kp.k: AlphaEvolve illustrates optimization through repeated guessing and checking
kp.d: Wei presents Google’s AlphaEvolve as a public example of exploiting cheap verification to optimize objectives, reporting mathematical and operational innovations without quantifying them. He uses fitting 11 unit hexagons inside the smallest outer hexagon as an illustrative problem meeting all five properties, then predicts that any solvable problem meeting those properties will be solved within the next few years.
qs: AlphaEvolve can be seen as a very clever instantiation of guess-and-check that allows for ruthless optimization of an objective, which has resulted in several mathematical and operational innovations.
Find the smallest outer hexagon that fits 11 unit hexagons.
Indeed, my belief is that any solvable problem that fits those five properties will be solved in the next few years.

kp.k: Scientific discovery can reward single-problem optimization
kp.d: Wei distinguishes optimizing an individual unsolved scientific problem from conventional machine learning’s emphasis on generalization to unseen problems. What might be described as overfitting can be valuable in this setting because solving the particular problem is itself the objective.
qs: One thing about the types of problems solved by AlphaEvolve is that it can be seen as “overfitting” to a single problem.
In traditional machine learning, we already know the labels in the training set and the significant test was to measure generalization to unseen problems.
in scientific innovation, we are in a totally different realm where we only care about solving a single problem (train=test!) because it’s an unsolved problem and potentially extremely valuable.

kp.k: Verifier’s rule does not promise computational efficiency
kp.d: Wei distinguishes his proposed rule from the open P = NP question: it does not specify how much time AI would require to solve a problem. He notes that solving competition mathematics can require far more computation than checking an answer against an existing answer key.
qs: While both P = NP and verifier’s rule discuss asymmetry of verification, verifier’s rule does not make any claims about the time it would take for AI to solve the problem.
it takes far more computation to solve the problem than to verify a solution given that we already have the answer key.

kp.k: Physical optimization depends on rapid, scalable measurement
kp.d: Wei extends the rule beyond computational tasks, predicting eventual AI optimization of catalysts and aerodynamic car designs if systems can measure outcomes quickly and at scale. The forecast is conditional on measurement infrastructure, not a report that these optimization goals have already been achieved.
qs: verifier’s rule also applies to non-computational tasks.

verifier’s rule would claim that AI would eventually be able to optimize non-computational endeavors like finding the best catalyst to speed up a chemical reaction, or the best aerodynamic car design for the fastest quarter-mile time, provided that we design the systems to measure those endeavors quickly and at scale.

kp.k: Uneven verifiability predicts uneven AI capabilities
kp.d: Wei concludes with a forecast that AI capabilities will develop unevenly, with substantially stronger performance on verifiable tasks because those tasks are easier to train systems to solve. The source does not translate this forecast into claims about particular legal occupations, service models or professional rules.
qs: We will likely have a jagged edge of intelligence, where AI is much smarter at verifiable tasks because it’s so much easier to solve verifiable tasks.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Jason Wei predicts that AI will solve solvable, easily verifiable tasks, with capabilities advancing unevenly in favour of tasks that provide effective training signals.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain AI source, not a claim about legal services. Wei's 'verifier’s rule' links ease of training to verifiability. He argues that advance preparation, such as answer keys and well-covered test cases, can make verification easier and thus improve the conditions for AI training. He predicts that solvable problems satisfying five verification properties will be solved in the next few years, and extends the argument to physical-world optimization if measurement can be made fast and scalable. Here verification means checking candidate solutions to generate feedback, not specifically human review of AI output before professional reliance.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Wei supports his predictions with qualitative observations about deep learning and benchmarks, illustrative tasks, and Google's AlphaEvolve; he provides no quantitative test of the general rule.
pts.d: Wei claims that measurable objectives have historically been amenable to optimization and that most proposed AI benchmarks are easy to verify and have been solved. He identifies AlphaEvolve as a public example of guess-and-check optimization producing mathematical and operational innovations. Sudoku, crosswords, BrowseComp, competition mathematics and coding tests illustrate differences between solving and checking effort. His explanation is that fast, scalable, low-noise feedback permits many informative gradient steps. These examples and the proposed mechanism support an explicitly stated belief, rather than a demonstrated universal result. No legal-sector evidence is offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The strongest forecast is 'in the next few years' from the 2025 source, conditional on solvability and five favourable verification properties; physical-world applications are framed as eventual.
pts.d: The five properties are objective agreement, verification within seconds, parallel scalability, low-noise correspondence with solution quality, and graded rewards. Wei notes that binary outcomes can yield continuous rewards by averaging across examples. He explicitly distinguishes his rule from a claim about computational solution time: solving may require far more computation than checking. Physical-world optimization depends on systems that measure outcomes quickly and at scale. His examples of essays and scientific hypotheses also qualify the broader picture: checking can be slower than proposing an answer, and advance preparation does not always make checking trivial.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The implications concern AI developers and users of AI in mathematical, software, scientific and engineering problem-solving; no legal roles or markets are identified.
pts.d: AI developers are implicated through Wei's argument that building effective verification environments enables reinforcement learning. Mathematical and operational problem-solvers are the beneficiaries illustrated by AlphaEvolve. Scientists and engineers are prospective beneficiaries of AI optimizing individual valuable problems, including catalysts and aerodynamic designs, when suitable measurement systems exist. These affected groups are inferred from his domain examples rather than an explicit labour-market analysis. Wei does not predict employment displacement, pricing changes, professional restructuring or legal-service outcomes.
